transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-05-21 15:00 PDT
- Duration: 53 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Moore (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Equinox Head of Platform), Lena Ortiz (Equinox CISO), Markus Reiss (Equinox Compliance), Julia Chen (Equinox Product Eng)

Summary:
Equinox is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted and private deployments. Primary concerns: keystore residency and routing (KMS vs HSM vs escrow), region-locking (GDPR/Euro customers), log retention and legal hold, and fallback behavior when a region or tenant must be isolated. They want clarification on what Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private actually means for cryptographic key control and audit evidence.

Topics discussed:
- Keystore ownership and routing (customer-managed KMS, HSM, and escrow)
- Region-locking and automatic fallback policies
- Log visibility, redaction, and retention windows for financial regulated data
- SOC 2 / HIPAA / GDPR implications for hosted vs private deployments
- Next steps: diagrams, bakeoff, security docs and compliance questionnaire

Action items (captured in metadata): see action_items field

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Moore: Hey everyone thanks for joining, looks like we have most of the folks on. I'm Alex Moore from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Priya Nair, our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Priya Nair: Hi all, hi. I'll go tech deep when we get into the keystore and routing stuff.
[00:12] Samir Patel: Thanks Alex, appreciate it. Quick intros - I'm Samir, Head of Platform at Equinox. Lena's our CISO, Markus does compliance, Julia's product.
[00:20] Lena Ortiz: Hi.
[00:21] Markus Reiss: Hello.
[00:22] Julia Chen: Hey.
[00:25] Alex Moore: Great. We planned this as a discovery to map your residency and key management constraints and walk through how Redwood's Hosted, Dedicated, and Private options map to those. Sound right?
[00:33] Samir Patel: Yes, and to be clear, we're not decided on configurations yet. Primary drivers: EU customers where data can't leave EU, some US healthcare customers (HIPAA) and overall auditability for transaction logs.
[00:45] Lena Ortiz: And crucially the keystore. We cannot hand keys to a third party for production PII/HIPAA — so we need see what control we have.
[00:53] Alex Moore: Absolutely. High level: Hosted API is the fastest but keys are Redwood-managed by default; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and options for customer-managed KMS integration; Private (VPC or on-prem) is where you can bring your own KMS/HSM and keep keys in your control. But the nuance is in routing and fallback — Priya, want to add?
[01:10] Priya Nair: Yeah, so in practice we support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private. For hosted we can offer bring-your-key for encrypting at rest in some scenarios but it depends on contractual and region constraints. Also, when you talk about fallback — Redwood can route to a region-specific model replica or degrade to a compatible model variant if primary region is unavailable; however that routing needs to be policy-defined so it doesn't cross a legal boundary.
[01:35] Markus Reiss: Ok so if we configure the policy 'EU-only' then requests from our US cluster can't fall back to US-hosted nodes?
[01:42] Priya Nair: Correct, if you set strict region-locking, our router will block cross-region fallback. There is also a graceful degrade option where you can route to a model with reduced capabilities but still within the allowed region.
[01:54] Julia Chen: Can you spell out the keystore flow for inference calls? We don't want plaintext data leaving our VPC or keys leaving our HSM.
[02:02] Alex Moore: Sure. Typical flows: 1) Customer-encrypted payloads where you encrypt client-side and Redwood sees ciphertext; 2) Customer-managed KMS where Redwood's control plane calls your KMS for envelope keys, keys never stored plaintext in Redwood; 3) For Private on-prem install, keys remain on-prem HSM and Redwood process runs inside your network. Note though some telemetry and minimal metadata can still be produced unless redaction is enabled.
[02:28] Lena Ortiz: That telemetry is the tricky part — we need evidence for audits without exposing PII. What does Redwood capture in logs by default?
[02:36] Priya Nair: Default logs include request metadata — timestamps, model used, token counts, latency, routing decision. We can configure log redaction and token-level suppression. For HIPAA customers we support a masked logging profile; for GDPR we also offer data subject request workflows and deletion hooks.
[02:52] Samir Patel: Are you able to provide per-tenant log partitioning so that we can hand off logs to internal auditors without exposing other tenants?
[02:59] Alex Moore: Yes, Dedicated and Private include tenant isolation for logs. Hosted can do logical partitions but the control plane is still Redwood-managed — if you require complete physical separation we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[03:12] Markus Reiss: About keystore escrow — we've been asked by legal whether we can support key escrow for long-term legal hold where keys are stored in a vault controlled by us but accessible via a formal process. Is that supported?
[03:22] Priya Nair: We do have an escrow pattern where keys can be escrowed in a customer-controlled HSM or a partner-managed escrow. We generally need to align on operational runbooks and the SLA for retrieval — that's something we'd document. There's sometimes confusion around the word "escrow" — is the vault on your side or a third party?
[03:35] Lena Ortiz: Ideally on our side, within our HSM cluster, but accessible to the Redwood runtime under strict ACLs and mTLS.
[03:43] Priya Nair: That fits the Private path best — Redwood runtime inside your VPC with mutual TLS to your keystore. For Dedicated we can also integrate to your KMS via private peering but the runtime still lives in Redwood-managed hosts.
[03:58] Alex Moore: I want to flag one subtlety: some of our hardware-backed acceleration (GPU inference kernels) is only available in certain regions or in our hosted pool. If you insist on region-lock and on-prem keys we may need to map to a compatible model quantization which affects latency/cost. We'll show tradeoffs in the diagram.
[04:16] Samir Patel: That tradeoff is acceptable as long as we get predictable latency numbers.
[04:19] Julia Chen: Can we do a short bakeoff with a representative prompt traffic pattern? Like 90/10 short vs long requests?
[04:25] Priya Nair: Absolutely — I can run a 48-hour sample on Dedicated and on a private deploy (if we can provide a fixture environment) and share latency percentiles and token costs.
[04:35] Lena Ortiz: On retention — we need retention windows per regulatory class. For transaction records we need 7 years, but our logs for debugging can be 90 days. Can Redwood provide configurable retention per log type?
[04:47] Alex Moore: Yes, logs and traces are configurable. We can set retention by channel — audit logs (immutable append-only) vs debug logs (short retention). We also offer legal hold flags to prevent deletion for specific records.
[04:58] Markus Reiss: About auditability — does Redwood provide signed evidence for model responses and log tamper-evidence?
[05:06] Priya Nair: We provide append-only audit trails and can sign artifacts with a key you trust. For the highest level of non-repudiation we'd recommend Private with your keystore for signing.
[05:15] Samir Patel: For GDPR, how does cross-border data subject access work if a EU subject requests deletion?
[05:22] Alex Moore: We have deletion hooks tied to your ID mapping — if you have identifiers in the payload we can build workflows to find and redact. Also region-locking reduces the risk of accidental copies in other regions.
[05:32] Lena Ortiz: A practical question — can we get the control plane logs (who changed policies) into our SIEM?
[05:38] Priya Nair: Yes — we can forward control plane events to your SIEM over syslog or to S3 a/c with signed delivery. There is an enterprise add-on for long-term retention and compliance export.
[05:48] Speaker 1: (unintelligible)
[05:50] Alex Moore: Quick check: are there any red lines — like a must-have that will force you to choose Private over Dedicated or Hosted?
[05:58] Markus Reiss: Must-haves: customer-controlled keys in an HSM for production PII and legal hold access only via formal process. Also physical residency for certain EU clients — no cross-border fallback allowed. If both are required, Private or dedicated with strict peering is likely.
[06:12] Samir Patel: And we need the ability for operations to pull signed evidence on demand for audits.
[06:18] Priya Nair: Noted. On the operations side, we can publish a runbook for retrieval and for emergency key rotation procedures.
[06:25] Julia Chen: One more thing — latency SLOs. If we keep everything in EU and keys on-prem, can you guarantee 100ms p95 for short prompts?
[06:34] Priya Nair: 100ms p95 is challenging if inference must traverse an on-prem HSM synchronously for each request. We often recommend envelope key patterns where KMS is used to unwrap session keys less frequently and then encrypted cache (KV cache) avoids per-token KMS hops. That gets you closer to 100ms. There may be a warmup/steady-state characteristic.
[06:54] Lena Ortiz: When you say KV cache can you confirm that KV cache content doesn't leak PII and is encryptable?
[07:00] Priya Nair: Yes the KV cache is encrypted at rest. We recommend you encrypt keys with your KMS so that even if cache is persisted, it remains encrypted and unreadable without your key. We call it prefix/KV caching but sometimes the transcript says KV cash ha, sorry.
[07:13] (laughter)
[07:15] Alex Moore: For legal hold — Markus, would you be ok if we included an appendix in the contract describing retrieval SLA and access control?
[07:22] Markus Reiss: Yes, that helps. Also we'll need the SOC 2 and ISO evidence; if possible, data flow diagrams that show where keys and logs live.
[07:31] Alex Moore: We'll attach SOC 2 and our ISO cert, plus a tailored data flow diagram.
[07:36] Samir Patel: Competitor check — we've been looking at Anthropic's managed endpoints and some self-hosted stacks. Is there differentiation here you want to call out?
[07:44] Priya Nair: The big difference is the unified serving runtime with routing policies and built-in fallback. Some providers are either pure hosted with limited key control or pure ops-only, requiring you to manage the runtime. Redwood tries to give flexible modes with consistent API and observability. But we'll be explicit about which acceleration features live where.
[08:03] Julia Chen: Ok practical next steps?
[08:06] Alex Moore: I'll share a region-lock diagram and keystore matrix by end of week. Priya will run a small bakeoff for a representative workload and share numbers. We'll also send the SOC 2 pack and a sample contract appendix for key escrow and legal hold.
[08:18] Lena Ortiz: Looking forward to those. Also please include a sample audit evidence bundle so our auditors can see the format.
[08:24] Alex Moore: Will do.
[08:26] (long pause, background noise)
[08:35] Priya Nair: One more note on the fallback behavior — we can add a policy that logs attempted cross-border fallbacks and send an alert to your security team.
[08:43] Lena Ortiz: That's good, we want alerting.
[08:45] Samir Patel: Timeline constraint — we hope to decide by mid-June so we'd need the bakeoff and docs in the next two weeks.
[08:53] Alex Moore: That's doable. We'll aim for the deadlines in the action items.
[08:58] Markus Reiss: A small technical question: does the control plane ever see plaintext keys or decrypted secrets?
[09:04] Priya Nair: No, not in the customer-managed KMS flow. The control plane sees metadata and envelope key references but not the raw symmetric keys. If you choose hosted with Redwood-managed keys we obviously have operational access but that requires contractual terms.
[09:19] Julia Chen: Could you also include an example of how SSO and RBAC map to our audit logs? We want to ensure user actions are traceable.
[09:27] Alex Moore: Yes, we'll include the SSO audit mapping.
[09:30] (voices checking calendar)
[09:34] Alex Moore: Any final questions before we wrap?
[09:36] Lena Ortiz: No, but please be explicit on encryption-at-rest and in-transit diagrams.
[09:40] Samir Patel: Also please call out where the performance hit is when using on-prem keys.
[09:45] Alex Moore: We'll do that. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and propose a time for a short bakeoff sync.
[09:53] Meeting ends.
